summary: A 3D scene from named primitives (box, sphere, cylinder, cone, torus, plane), each with a size, a position, a rotation and a theme colour: the server frames them with a camera that fits every angle at any window shape, lights them, and adds drag to orbit, autorotate and an assembly animation. No 3D maths for the caller. Plays in the C++ and TypeScript players; 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming).

objects.doc: One entry per part: {"shape": "box", "size": [w, h, d], "at": [x, y, z], "color": "@colors.primary"}. Units are yours (metres, cm: the camera adapts), Y up, X right, Z toward the viewer; `at` is the centre of the part's box. Shapes: box (size [w, h, d]; "round": r for rounded edges), sphere (size = diameter, or [x, y, z] for an ellipsoid), cylinder and cone (size [diameter, height]; a cone's apex points along its axis), torus (size [outer diameter, tube thickness], lying flat), plane (size [w, d], lying flat, seen from above). Optional: "axis": "x" | "z" | "-y" ... turns a round shape (a cylinder with axis "z" faces the viewer like a speaker cone), "rotate": [rx, ry, rz] degrees, "from": [dx, dy, dz] where the part starts in the assembly animation (default: away from the centre), "step": parts with the same step move together. Up to 40 parts

label.doc: What the scene shows, for a screen reader: "A bookshelf assembling itself"

orbit.doc: Drag to turn the scene (left-right spins it, up-down tilts it within tiltRange); it coasts to a stop

autorotate.doc: Turns on its own, in degrees per second (20 is a slow turntable; negative turns the other way). Repaints every frame while shown. Off in mono

spin.doc: The starting view, degrees around the vertical axis: 0 is straight on, -30 shows the front and the right side

tilt.doc: The starting view, degrees looking down from above: 0 is level, 20 shows the top a little

tiltRange.doc: How far a drag may tilt, [low, high] in degrees (within -89 to 89). The camera frames every angle in this range, so a wider range leaves the scene smaller

assemble.doc: Assembly animation: the parts fly in one after another (in list order, or by `step`), the whole holds, then flies apart and repeats. Each part starts at its `from` offset. In mono the scene shows assembled and still

stagger.doc: Seconds between one step's start and the next one's

hold.doc: Seconds the assembled whole holds before it flies apart

frame.doc: What the camera keeps in view: the assembled object, or also the parts at their start offsets. auto: all with assemble, else assembled

light.doc: studio: a key light from the upper left and a cool fill from the right (product shot). soft: three lights, no dark faces. flat: from the front, faces close to their colour (diagrams)

style.doc: solid: lit faces. outlined: lit faces with their edges drawn in lineColor (a technical look). wireframe: only the edges, in each part's colour. Mono is always background faces with onSurface edges

floor.doc: A thin disc under the scene, in floorColor (a turntable)

fill.doc: The fraction of the view the scene may reach at its widest reachable angle (0.3 to 1)

insetTop.doc: dp kept clear at the top for the overlay (a title): the scene is framed in the window's height minus the insets and moved below it, at every window size

insetBottom.doc: dp kept clear at the bottom for the overlay (a caption, a button)

background.doc: The window behind the scene; also the faces' fill in mono

lineColor.doc: Edges in the outlined style and in mono

overlay.doc: Nodes drawn over the scene (a title, a caption, a button), in a box that fills the window: align them with a column or modifiers, and keep their room clear with insetTop / insetBottom. The 3D always fills the window behind them

Scene3D.label: A blue cube on a grey slab

pitfalls: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): the scene plays in the C++ and TypeScript players (rc2image, the web player, the MCP renders) and the Java JSON parser drops its 3D operations. Don't use it for a screen that must play on Android today

Scene3D fills the window: the players draw 3D into a window-sized buffer placed at the canvas's top left, so a 3D canvas in a column or beside other content is drawn off-centre and spills out of its box. Put titles and captions in the overlay slot and reserve their height with insetTop / insetBottom (dp), so the scene is framed below them
Name parts, don't compute views: give sizes and centres in the object's own units; the camera, the tilt and spin and the framing are the server's. Don't add your own camera3D or matrix3D around it

Each part is drawn in software every frame: keep to about 30 parts (each costs about 60 to 90 B and a few ms per frame on a phone-sized window); spheres, cylinders and tori are 100 to 600 triangles each, boxes 12

Colours are theme colours lit by the preset: a light part on the light background (surface on background) loses its edges; use outline, surfaceHigh, muted, primary and secondary for bodies, or style outlined
autorotate and assemble repaint every frame for as long as the scene is shown (continuousSec); leave both off for a still product shot that only moves when dragged
A plane is single-sided (seen from above); for a panel seen from both sides use a thin box
